title: Origins and History of Aviator Sunglasses
body:
The Aviator Sunglasses belongs to the 1936–present era and traces to Bausch & Lomb.

The Wrights flew at Kitty Hawk (1903) after solving control with wing-warping; Europe caught up fast (Santos-Dumont, Blériot's 1909 Channel crossing). WWI made the airplane a weapon: Fokker's interrupter gear, the Red Baron's circus, bombers over London. The 1920s: barnstormers, airmail (1926), Lindbergh's 1927 Atlantic solo. The DC-3 (1935) made airlines profitable; the 1930s streamlined everything. WWII's aircraft (Spitfire, Mustang, B-17, Zero) were the war's cutting edge; jets (Me 262, 1944) arrived at the end. Postwar: the 707 (1958) jet age, the 747 (1970), Concorde (1976–2003) — supersonic transport's brief glory. Airships: Zeppelin's rigid ships, the Hindenburg disaster (1937), the American blimp program.

Within that longer story, Aviator Sunglasses: The 1936; the 1937's. The Aviator is the pilot's shade.

title: How Aviator Sunglasses Works
body:
Wings make lift by deflecting air downward (angle of attack + camber); the Wrights' genius was three-axis control (warp/ailerons, rudder, elevator). Piston engines (rotary, radial, inline) turned propellers; superchargers kept power at altitude. Jets (turbojet, then turbofan) compress, burn, and exhaust air for thrust. Airships lift with hydrogen/helium in rigid (Zeppelin) or pressure (blimp) envelopes. Navigation went from pilotage (following railroads) to radio ranges, VOR, and inertial.

Applied to the Aviator Sunglasses (1936–present, Bausch & Lomb): The Aviator is the pilot's shade.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Aviation History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of aviation history:

• lift / drag / thrust / weight — The four forces.
• angle of attack — Wing vs airflow; stall's trigger.
• wing-warping — The Wrights' roll control.
• deadstick — Engine-out landing.

• supercharger — Altitude power for piston engines.

• rigid airship — Zeppelin's duralumin skeleton.
• blimp — Non-rigid pressure airship.

Aviation is the century's romance: the barnstormer's dare, Lindbergh's ticker tape, the Spitfire's elliptical wing, the 747's hump. 'The friendly skies' were once glamorous — stewardesses, cocktail lounges, the Concorde's champagne at 60,000 feet. The Hindenburg's flames are newsreel's most famous footage. Every airport kid pressing against the glass inherits it.

title: Aviator Sunglasses — Lift, weight, and range estimator (Runnable Python)
body:
Estimates lift requirements, stall speed, and still-air range — the back-of-envelope math of classic aircraft design.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Aviator Sunglasses so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Classic aircraft math: lift, stall, range (public-domain formulas)
import math

def stall_speed_mph(weight_lb, wing_area_sqft, cl_max=1.4):
    # Vs = sqrt(2W / (rho * S * Cl)) in ft/s, rho=0.002377
    v_fps = math.sqrt(2 * weight_lb / (0.002377 * wing_area_sqft * cl_max))
    return v_fps * 0.681818

# J-3 Cub-ish: 1220 lb, 178 sqft
print(f"J-3 Cub stall: ~{stall_speed_mph(1220, 178):.0f} mph")
# DC-3-ish: 25000 lb, 987 sqft
print(f"DC-3 stall: ~{stall_speed_mph(25000, 987, 1.6):.0f} mph")

def range_sm(fuel_gal, gph, cruise_mph, reserve_hr=0.75):
    return (fuel_gal / gph - reserve_hr) * cruise_mph
print(f"Cub range (36gal, 5gph, 75mph): ~{range_sm(36, 5, 75):.0f} sm")
